currentContext.strengths: Integrated business model encompassing ethical sourcing, advanced processing, product innovation and value-added solution development, with a fully integrated single-site facility at Birkoni spanning milling, solvent extraction, refining, fractionation, interesterification and packing.|DSIR-recognised Milcoa Innovation & Research Centre with application development capability; 11 new products and developments delivered during FY26 (5 new products, 6 new developments) across five branded platforms.|Access to underutilised forest raw materials through long-term partnerships with tribal collectors, women-led cooperatives and rural communities across India and West Africa, supported by fair-trade practices and traceability systems.|Backward integration at origin through ten wholly owned subsidiaries across West Africa, the UAE and Brazil, securing exotic oilseed procurement and supply-chain resilience.|Breadth of internationally recognised quality, food-safety, ethical-trade and sustainability certifications that support access to demanding multinational customers.|Co-development approach with global brands producing customised, application-specific formulations, which supports the shift of sales towards value-added products.|Recognition as a Three Star Export House by the Government of India and, in 2016, as the highest processor and exporter of Sal seed and Mango kernel.
currentContext.strategies: Acquire and maintain a leadership position in chosen areas of business by continuously innovating products and adopting a co-development approach for various applications and categories through continuous R&D and collaboration.|Become the most preferred and first-choice solution provider for tree-borne specialty fats and butters.|Deliver a fully integrated solution spanning ethical collection of tree-borne oilseeds in partnership with tribal communities, advanced processing of Cocoa Butter Equivalents and specialty fats and butters, and their application into final products.|Operate an integrated value chain spanning ethical sourcing, processing, refining, fractionation, product development and global distribution to deliver quality, traceability, consistency and customisation at every stage.|Build international presence through wholly owned subsidiaries across West Africa, the UAE and Brazil to secure sourcing and serve global customers.|Pursue the 'Growth for Development' philosophy — 'Waste to Wealth', 'Poorest to Richest' and 'Forest to Fortune Brands' — combining sustainability with innovation, and enhance the livelihood of tribal communities through CSR in health, sanitation and education.|Expand the contribution of value-added products and premium filling fats launched via Milcoa® R&D.
currentContext.expansion: During FY26 Manorama strengthened its operating platform through capacity enhancement, international expansion and strategic investments. The principal operational milestone was the debottlenecking of Solvent Fractionation Plant 2 (SF2), which lifted its capacity by 30% from 25,000 MTPA to 32,500 MTPA and raised total fractionation capacity to 47,500 MTPA, creating additional flexibility to serve demand for value-added specialty fat solutions; packaging capacity was also expanded during the year. Management describes existing capacity as having operated at strong utilisation levels. Looking forward, the Company has initiated a strategic capex programme of approximately Rs 460 crore designed to strengthen both forward integration (specialty fats, CBEs and value-added formulations) and backward integration (securing access to critical raw materials at origin), described as the FY28 growth platform. In India this comprises a new 75,000 MTPA Solvent Fractionation Facility (SF3), a new 90,000 MTPA refinery and a new 75,000 MTPA Cocoa Butter Alternative (CBA) facility, all stated to be under development. In Burkina Faso a new Shea and Mango processing facility of approximately 90,000 MTPA is planned, supported by an MoU signed with the Government of Burkina Faso. Internationally, the operationalisation of wholly owned subsidiary Taang Kaam Industries SA strengthened the Company's presence in a major shea-producing region and advanced its backward-integration strategy, while the successful completion of the first commercial production batch through Manorama Latin America LTDA / Dekel established a platform for future growth across Latin America. Historically, the earlier capacity build included a 30,000 MTPA refinery, 30,000 MTPA expeller and 15,000 MTPA interesterification capacity commissioned in 2023, and a new 25,000 MTPA solvent fractionation plant commissioned in 2024 that took total fractionation capacity from 15,000 MTPA to 40,000 MTPA.
currentContext.mdna: Indian specialty fats and butter demand continued to grow during 2025-26 on rising demand from bakery, confectionery, dairy, infant nutrition and processed food sectors, aided by urbanisation, changing consumption patterns, rising disposable incomes and expansion of organised food processing.|Management states the outlook for the specialty fats and butter industry remains encouraging and that demand for cocoa butter equivalents, specialty butters and customised fat solutions is expected to remain strong, supported by growth in chocolate and bakery consumption; with its diversified portfolio, expanding capacities and focus on innovation and sustainable sourcing, Manorama says it is well positioned to capitalise on these opportunities.|Volatile cocoa prices are pushing manufacturers toward CBE/CBS, which the Company notes reduces ingredient cost by 30-40% while maintaining quality — a structural driver of cocoa butter alternative adoption.|Rising health awareness is increasing demand for low trans-fat, non-hydrogenated and plant-based alternatives, with consumers seeking clean-label specialty fats.|Fat modification technologies — fractionation, interesterification and enzymatic processing — are enabling customised fat profiles for specific applications, favouring technically capable suppliers.|Government policy support: in October 2024 the Indian government approved a USD 1.2 Bn programme to boost domestic edible oil output from 12.7 MT to 25.45 MT by 2030-31.|India remains one of the largest consumers of edible oils globally, with annual edible oil consumption estimated at approximately 24-25 Mn tonnes (IVPA), supported by rising food processing activity and packaged/convenience food consumption.|Indian specialty fats and oils market valued at approximately USD 1.9 Bn in 2025, projected to reach USD 2.8 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of approximately 4.29% during 2026-2034 (IMARC Group).|Indian chocolate market valued at approximately USD 1.80 Bn in 2024 and projected to reach USD 2.99 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 5.20% (Expert Market Research); outlook stated as positive, expected to drive sustained demand for CBEs, CBSs and specialty fats used in chocolate manufacturing.|Milk chocolate dominates the Indian chocolate market on affordability and acceptance, while dark chocolate is among the fastest-growing segments on health consciousness and premium demand, and white chocolate is a niche but expanding segment.|Global confectionery market estimated between USD 220.85 Bn and USD 228.30 Bn in 2026, reaching USD 295.06 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 3.26%, supported by premiumisation, emerging-market demand and product innovation; raw material price volatility remains the industry's primary structural headwind.|Global cosmetics market valued at USD 354.68 Bn in 2025, projected to grow from USD 375.62 Bn in 2026 to USD 644.17 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 6.97%, with Asia Pacific holding 40.16% share in 2025 and skincare the top category at 35.13%; growth drivers include rising self-care awareness and a shift to organic, vegan and naturally formulated cosmetics.|Global HoReCa market estimated by The Business Research Company at USD 3,304.71 Bn in 2025 and USD 3,527.87 Bn in 2026 (up 6.8% year-on-year), forecast to reach USD 4,561.91 Bn by 2030 at a CAGR of 6.6%, driven by tourism recovery, urbanisation, rising disposable incomes, expansion of food service outlets and digital innovation.|India's HoReCa sector entered 2025-26 as one of the fastest-growing institutional food and hospitality markets in Asia Pacific, estimated by Market Research Future at USD 250.22 Bn in 2024.|Premiumisation across developed markets combined with volume expansion in developing economies of Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Latin America is expected to sustain above-trend chocolate and confectionery consumption growth in those geographies.

risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a material risk. The Company relies on digital systems for managing operations, supply chain traceability, customer interactions and compliance processes, making it vulnerable to data breaches, cyberattacks and unauthorised access. Financial implication stated as negative: cyber incidents or data breaches may lead to operational disruptions, data loss, regulatory penalties and reputational damage. Mitigations include a comprehensive Cybersecurity Policy covering network security, access controls and data handling, security controls for confidential and personal data, senior-leadership oversight and continuous monitoring, internal audits and independent third-party assessments, data backup and retention protocols, annual cybersecurity training, and strengthened incident management.

risks.risk: Evolving data protection and compliance regulation
risks.note: The AR states that evolving data protection regulations and increasing stakeholder expectations for data security further heighten the risk of non-compliance, operational disruption and reputational impact — a compliance burden that grows with the Company's international footprint.

The entire product base begins with tree-borne seeds — Sal, Shea, Mango, Kokum, Mowrah and other exotic seeds — responsibly sourced from forest ecosystems across India and the shea-growing regions of West Africa. Availability and quality of these raw materials at origin is therefore structural to the business model.

As Manorama expands its global sourcing network, its framework is explicitly described as designed to manage supply chain risks and uphold internationally recognised environmental and social standards across sourcing regions. The Company continued implementing its No Deforestation, No Peat and No Exploitation (NDPE) commitments and relies on human rights due diligence, supplier onboarding, screening and periodic evaluations, technology-enabled audit and supplier monitoring, and traceability systems aligned with ISO 22000:2018 — indicating that lapses in sourcing conduct would carry commercial and reputational consequences.

risks.risk: Geographic dispersion of operations and sourcing
risks.note: The Company operates ten global subsidiaries and an international presence across India, West Africa, the UAE and Brazil, keeping it close to raw material origins but exposing it to the operational, regulatory and oversight complexity of multiple jurisdictions.

risks.risk: Dependence on customer-specific technical qualification and long-cycle collaboration
risks.note: Products are developed alongside customers and their technical teams to precise functional, sensory and performance requirements, and the Company serves a diverse industrial base across confectionery, chocolate, food, cosmetics and feed applications requiring consistent quality and customised solutions. This co-development model creates switching friction in the Company's favour but makes revenue dependent on retaining a limited set of qualifying industrial customers, managed through structured feedback, complaint tracking, CAPA processes and Voice of Customer surveys.

risks.risk: Regulatory and policy environment for sustainable sourcing and agri-based industries
risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table treats engagement with policymakers, industry bodies and regulatory institutions as a way to reduce compliance uncertainty and safeguard business continuity, implying that regulations governing sustainable sourcing, agri-based industries and ESG practices are a live variable for the business.

The AR states that forward-looking statements are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially, that certain data has been obtained from external sources the Company has not independently verified, and that past performance is not an indicator of future results.

one-line thesis: Manorama Industries delivered exceptional FY26 with 76% revenue growth and 27% EBITDA margins driven by volume surge and high-value CBE mix (now 30% of sales), while initiating a INR 460 Cr capex cycle for African backward integration and forward capacity expansion to sustain >25% growth trajectory through FY28.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 1,358 Cr (+76% YoY); EBITDA: INR 368 Cr (27.1% margin, +40bps YoY); PAT: INR 233 Cr (17.2% margin, normalized for INR 23.3 Cr cumulative FX MTM loss); Order Book: Not disclosed (demand-led production); Net Debt: INR ~200 Cr (Debt/Equity 0.38x), One-offs: INR 23.3 Cr FX MTM provision, INR ~13.5 Cr subsidiary startup losses.
guidance: Revenue Growth: >25% (FY27); Margin: Sustain 25%-27% EBITDA; Order Inflow: Strong visibility from global F&B/Cosmetic demand; Capex: INR 460 Cr over 2-3 years (commissioning by FY28).
order book & pipeline: Demand-led model with 85%-90% utilization target on expanded 52k TPA capacity; no formal order book disclosed but visibility high via long-term customer partnerships.
segment / subsidiary detail: CBE contributed ~30% of revenue (up from 10% two years ago); Stearin + CBE constitute 70%-75% of value-added mix; Solvent Fractionation Plant 2 debottlenecked to 32.5k TPA (+30%), Plant 1 (15k TPA) to follow; Total input capacity heading to 52k TPA.
growth verticals / optionality: Burkina Faso plant (INR 120 Cr) for seed-to-butter conversion (45%-60% RM cost savings, yield improvement); New 75k TPA Solvent Fractionation Plant 3 + CBE facility + 200 TPD refinery (INR 330-340 Cr) for forward integration; Targeting INR 3,500 Cr revenue by FY30.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin pressure in consolidated entities (43% vs 48% prior) due to subsidiary startup costs/freight; Standalone margins stable at ~48%; Expect normalization as subsidiaries scale; Logistic cost savings from Africa integration to offset freight inflation.
capex / expansion: INR 460 Cr total (INR 52 Cr spent in FY26); INR 120 Cr for Burkina Faso backward integration; INR 330-340 Cr for forward integration (CBE, Fractionation, Refinery); Phased commissioning by FY28; Funded via internal accruals (INR 260 Cr operating cash flow) and existing cash (INR 130 Cr FD); QIP (INR 500 Cr) is enabling only, not immediate.
capital allocation: Prioritizing high-ROCE capex (>6x asset turn expected on forward projects); Working capital cycle improved to 125 days (from 151); ROCE 33.6%, ROE 40.3%; No dividend change discussed, focus on reinvestment.
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical tension (West Africa, West Asia) impacting freight/energy; FX volatility (60% hedged, 40% open); Subsidiary ramp-up delays; Raw material price fluctuation (Shea, Sal, Mango).
management quality / tone: Highly confident, execution-focused, emphasizing long-term vision over quarterly noise; transparent on subsidiary losses as transitional; aggressive on capacity utilization and margin sustainability.
non-obvious takeaways: Annual cash profit (PAT+Dep) of INR 259 Cr now exceeds gross block (INR 250 Cr), signaling extreme capital efficiency; Burkina Faso project is government-backed (MoU signed) mitigating political risk; Immediate seed processing in Africa improves fat yield vs. 60-day transport lag.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Cocoa Butter Equivalents and specialty fats:** CBE (Cocoa Butter Equivalent), Stearin, Olein, Refined Butter
- **Filling and coating fats (Milcocream / Milcoat platforms):** Milcocream 1059 (all-round filling fat solution), Milcocream 1068 (bake-stable filling fat), Milcocream MF69 (milk fat replacer), Milcocream FF77 (palm-free fat development), Milcocream TF76 (trans-free fat development), Milcocream BS65 (bakery-focused specialty fat), Milcocream P56 (all-round filling fat), Milcoat 58NH (coating fat for confectionery applications)
- **Dipping and spreadable fats:** Milcodip MP35 (multipurpose specialty fat for frozen dessert), Milcodip MP65 (dipping and coating fat solution), Milcospread TU52 (spreadable fat for food applications)
- **Product platforms:** Milcocream, Milcoat, Milcolin, Milcodip, Milcospread
- **By-products:** De-oiled cake (cattle feed), Byproducts / gums

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: Demand-led model with 85%-90% utilization target on expanded 52k TPA capacity; no formal order book disclosed but visibility high via long-term customer partnerships.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: >25% (FY27); Margin: Sustain 25%-27% EBITDA; Order Inflow: Strong visibility from global F&B/Cosmetic demand; Capex: INR 460 Cr over 2-3 years (commissioning by FY28).

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Burkina Faso plant (INR 120 Cr) for seed-to-butter conversion (45%-60% RM cost savings, yield improvement); New 75k TPA Solvent Fractionation Plant 3 + CBE facility + 200 TPD refinery (INR 330-340 Cr) for forward integration; Targeting INR 3,500 Cr revenue by FY30.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian specialty fats and butter demand continued to grow during 2025-26 on rising demand from bakery, confectionery, dairy, infant nutrition and processed food sectors, aided by urbanisation, changing consumption patterns, rising disposable incomes and expansion of organised food processing.
- Management states the outlook for the specialty fats and butter industry remains encouraging and that demand for cocoa butter equivalents, specialty butters and customised fat solutions is expected to remain strong, supported by growth in chocolate and bakery consumption; with its diversified portfolio, expanding capacities and focus on innovation and sustainable sourcing, Manorama says it is well positioned to capitalise on these opportunities.
- Volatile cocoa prices are pushing manufacturers toward CBE/CBS, which the Company notes reduces ingredient cost by 30-40% while maintaining quality — a structural driver of cocoa butter alternative adoption.
- Rising health awareness is increasing demand for low trans-fat, non-hydrogenated and plant-based alternatives, with consumers seeking clean-label specialty fats.
- Fat modification technologies — fractionation, interesterification and enzymatic processing — are enabling customised fat profiles for specific applications, favouring technically capable suppliers.
- Government policy support: in October 2024 the Indian government approved a USD 1.2 Bn programme to boost domestic edible oil output from 12.7 MT to 25.45 MT by 2030-31.
- India remains one of the largest consumers of edible oils globally, with annual edible oil consumption estimated at approximately 24-25 Mn tonnes (IVPA), supported by rising food processing activity and packaged/convenience food consumption.
- Indian specialty fats and oils market valued at approximately USD 1.9 Bn in 2025, projected to reach USD 2.8 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of approximately 4.29% during 2026-2034 (IMARC Group).
- Indian chocolate market valued at approximately USD 1.80 Bn in 2024 and projected to reach USD 2.99 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 5.20% (Expert Market Research); outlook stated as positive, expected to drive sustained demand for CBEs, CBSs and specialty fats used in chocolate manufacturing.
- Milk chocolate dominates the Indian chocolate market on affordability and acceptance, while dark chocolate is among the fastest-growing segments on health consciousness and premium demand, and white chocolate is a niche but expanding segment.
- Global confectionery market estimated between USD 220.85 Bn and USD 228.30 Bn in 2026, reaching USD 295.06 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 3.26%, supported by premiumisation, emerging-market demand and product innovation; raw material price volatility remains the industry's primary structural headwind.
- Global cosmetics market valued at USD 354.68 Bn in 2025, projected to grow from USD 375.62 Bn in 2026 to USD 644.17 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 6.97%, with Asia Pacific holding 40.16% share in 2025 and skincare the top category at 35.13%; growth drivers include rising self-care awareness and a shift to organic, vegan and naturally formulated cosmetics.
- Global HoReCa market estimated by The Business Research Company at USD 3,304.71 Bn in 2025 and USD 3,527.87 Bn in 2026 (up 6.8% year-on-year), forecast to reach USD 4,561.91 Bn by 2030 at a CAGR of 6.6%, driven by tourism recovery, urbanisation, rising disposable incomes, expansion of food service outlets and digital innovation.
- India's HoReCa sector entered 2025-26 as one of the fastest-growing institutional food and hospitality markets in Asia Pacific, estimated by Market Research Future at USD 250.22 Bn in 2024.
- Premiumisation across developed markets combined with volume expansion in developing economies of Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Latin America is expected to sustain above-trend chocolate and confectionery consumption growth in those geographies.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Gross margin pressure in consolidated entities (43% vs 48% prior) due to subsidiary startup costs/freight; Standalone margins stable at ~48%; Expect normalization as subsidiaries scale; Logistic cost savings from Africa integration to offset freight inflation.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Prioritizing high-ROCE capex (>6x asset turn expected on forward projects); Working capital cycle improved to 125 days (from 151); ROCE 33.6%, ROE 40.3%; No dividend change discussed, focus on reinvestment.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: During FY26 Manorama strengthened its operating platform through capacity enhancement, international expansion and strategic investments. The principal operational milestone was the debottlenecking of Solvent Fractionation Plant 2 (SF2), which lifted its capacity by 30% from 25,000 MTPA to 32,500 MTPA and raised total fractionation capacity to 47,500 MTPA, creating additional flexibility to serve demand for value-added specialty fat solutions; packaging capacity was also expanded during the year. Management describes existing capacity as having operated at strong utilisation levels. Looking forward, the Company has initiated a strategic capex programme of approximately Rs 460 crore designed to strengthen both forward integration (specialty fats, CBEs and value-added formulations) and backward integration (securing access to critical raw materials at origin), described as the FY28 growth platform. In India this comprises a new 75,000 MTPA Solvent Fractionation Facility (SF3), a new 90,000 MTPA refinery and a new 75,000 MTPA Cocoa Butter Alternative (CBA) facility, all stated to be under development. In Burkina Faso a new Shea and Mango processing facility of approximately 90,000 MTPA is planned, supported by an MoU signed with the Government of Burkina Faso. Internationally, the operationalisation of wholly owned subsidiary Taang Kaam Industries SA strengthened the Company's presence in a major shea-producing region and advanced its backward-integration strategy, while the successful completion of the first commercial production batch through Manorama Latin America LTDA / Dekel established a platform for future growth across Latin America. Historically, the earlier capacity build included a 30,000 MTPA refinery, 30,000 MTPA expeller and 15,000 MTPA interesterification capacity commissioned in 2023, and a new 25,000 MTPA solvent fractionation plant commissioned in 2024 that took total fractionation capacity from 15,000 MTPA to 40,000 MTPA.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Highly confident, execution-focused, emphasizing long-term vision over quarterly noise; transparent on subsidiary losses as transitional; aggressive on capacity utilization and margin sustainability.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrated business model encompassing ethical sourcing, advanced processing, product innovation and value-added solution development, with a fully integrated single-site facility at Birkoni spanning milling, solvent extraction, refining, fractionation, interesterification and packing.
- DSIR-recognised Milcoa Innovation & Research Centre with application development capability; 11 new products and developments delivered during FY26 (5 new products, 6 new developments) across five branded platforms.
- Access to underutilised forest raw materials through long-term partnerships with tribal collectors, women-led cooperatives and rural communities across India and West Africa, supported by fair-trade practices and traceability systems.
- Backward integration at origin through ten wholly owned subsidiaries across West Africa, the UAE and Brazil, securing exotic oilseed procurement and supply-chain resilience.
- Breadth of internationally recognised quality, food-safety, ethical-trade and sustainability certifications that support access to demanding multinational customers.
- Co-development approach with global brands producing customised, application-specific formulations, which supports the shift of sales towards value-added products.
- Recognition as a Three Star Export House by the Government of India and, in 2016, as the highest processor and exporter of Sal seed and Mango kernel.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Geopolitical tension (West Africa, West Asia) impacting freight/energy; FX volatility (60% hedged, 40% open); Subsidiary ramp-up delays; Raw material price fluctuation (Shea, Sal, Mango).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Annual cash profit (PAT+Dep) of INR 259 Cr now exceeds gross block (INR 250 Cr), signaling extreme capital efficiency; Burkina Faso project is government-backed (MoU signed) mitigating political risk; Immediate seed processing in Africa improves fat yield vs. 60-day transport lag.
